newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Helsinki might leave Romania in the cold-papers.
newsitem.headline: Helsinki might leave Romania in the cold-papers.

text.p: Romanian newspapers on Thursday voiced suspicions that the U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki might cut a new deal on NATO's expansion which would leave their country out in the cold.
"The fate of eastern Europe is being decided on the shores of Finland," ran a headline in the independent newspaper Adevarul.
"Clinton and Yeltsin are redrawing the map of the world," echoed the Ziua daily.
The summit between Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin is being dominated by NATO enlargement, with Russia stressing its fierce opposition to bringing in any new members.
Romania is lobbying hard for inclusion in the first wave of expansion to be announced at an Alliance summit in July.
But despite the election last year of a centrist government viewed more favourably in the West, it is seen as a longshot behind favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Romanian media have drawn parallels between the Helsinki summit and the 1945 Yalta conference at which the leaders of the United States, Britain and Soviet Union set the foundations for divided Cold War Europe.

Ziua said on Thursday that "Romania should not fall again under the scissors of history", prompting a protest from the Russian embassy decrying its "irreverent" language and the poor post-Soviet relations between Moscow and Bucharest.

"To Russia, Romania is an important country," the embassy said in a note issued to media. It called the Ziua story "an insult to Russian foreign policy," and urged Romanian media not to jeopardise moves to improve ties.
Romania has signed no treaties with its three main ex-Soviet neighbours to the east, Russia, Ukraine and Moldova.
Talks have stalled on Bucharest's insistence that Moscow atone publicly for the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact under which the Kremlin seized large chunks of Romanian territory.
A treaty with Ukraine is viewed in the West as vital to Romania's NATO membership bid and considerable progress has been made in working out provisions acceptable to both sides.
But matters are moving more slowly with Russia.
Russian ambassador Yevgeny Ostrovenko this week told the pro-government daily Romania Libera the 1939 treaty was a "closed chapter".
